product.title: Arabic 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 in Modern Standard Arabic (Fusha): every line of Arabic fully vowelled, with a pronunciation guide under each line of dialogue, word-for-word translations that show how Arabic builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of all 28 letters with their joined forms, the vowel marks, sun and moon letters, an A1 summary of case endings, full past- and present-tense verb tables, and a list of the most frequent verbs. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from sentences with no word for "is" to the idafa that must never take ال.

blocks.text: Many learners come to this book having already met the Arabic script — perhaps from Qur'an classes, travel, or a family background — and can already sound out اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ or recognize ب, ت, ث without thinking. If that's you, that head start will save you weeks. If you're starting from zero, don't worry: the first chapters take you through the alphabet step by step.

But that head start can also mislead, and it's important to be honest about it on page one. Reading is not understanding. Many people learn to pronounce Arabic letters in order to recite correctly — and that is an entirely different skill from understanding a sentence. The eye learns to recognize shapes, while the ear and the mind are never asked: what does this word mean, and why does its ending change?

So this book will use whatever you already have without pretending you're halfway there. The first chapters go over the letters once more — this time with their joined forms and the sounds that separate س from ص — and then we go straight into sentences.

The language you're learning here is **Fusha**, or *Modern Standard Arabic*. It's the language of Al Jazeera news, books, official letters, sermons, and writing across the whole Arab world from Morocco to Oman. People in Cairo and Amman don't use it to joke around at a café — for that they have their own dialects — but both write, read and give speeches in the same Fusha. One language for twenty-two countries: that's why we start with Fusha.

Three things trip up English-speaking learners most, and all three are set up in the early units and practiced again right up to the last. **First, sentences without "is".** أَنَا طَالِبٌ is literally just "I student", and that is already a complete sentence. **Second, every noun has a gender.** A table is feminine, a book is masculine, and that choice decides the form of the adjective, the demonstrative, even the verb. **Third, three-letter roots.** كَتَبَ (wrote), كِتَاب (book), مَكْتَب (desk), مَكْتَبَة (library), كَاتِب (writer) — all grow from one root, ك-ت-ب. Once you see the pattern, your vocabulary stops growing one word at a time and starts growing in clusters.

blocks.title: What this book does NOT teach — and why
items: **Full case endings (i'rab).** Arabic changes word endings according to their role in the sentence (ٌ ـ, َ ـ, ٍ ـ). At A1 it's enough to recognize them when reading, without having to add them yourself in every sentence. The ones you need to use actively are flagged in the unit notes.

**Dialect.** "Kaifa haaluka?" will sound a bit formal on the streets of Cairo, and that's fine: every Arab understands Fusha, and Fusha is what you can take to the entire Arab world at once. Dialects are much easier to pick up once the framework is in place.

blocks.text: The twenty units inside cover the whole framework of A1 Arabic: greeting and introducing yourself, saying where you're from and what you do, pointing at things, possession, numbers and prices, time and the clock, daily routines, ordering food, shopping, asking the way, talking about yesterday, and making plans.

Each unit is one study session: twenty to thirty minutes. The dialogues are short and deliberately sound like real conversation. Under each line is the pronunciation, then a natural English translation, then a **literal** translation — the Arabic word order forced into English. That last one often sounds odd, and that's exactly the point.
Enjoy your studies. بِالتَّوْفِيقِ! *(bittaufiiq — good luck)*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This book works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones set up.

blocks.text: This book follows the Assimil method: you don't memorize a list of rules and then try to build sentences; you absorb whole sentences first and let the rules follow. That's why the order in which you work through each unit matters.
Six steps for one unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, out loud, without looking at the meaning.** All the Arabic in this book is fully vowelled, so there isn't a single word whose sound you have to guess. Sound first, meaning later.

**Read it again, looking at the lines underneath.** The second line (small green letters) is the pronunciation, the third is natural English, the fourth (in italics) is a word-for-word **literal** translation that follows the Arabic order.

**Read the notes.** That's where the real content of the book is. The notes explain why a sentence is built the way it is, and almost always point out one mistake typical of English-speaking learners.
**Read the grammar box**, then go back to the dialogue and find the examples. A rule you've just read sticks much better when you find the evidence in the sentences yourself.
**Do the exercises on paper, not in your head.** Writing Arabic by hand is the fastest way to lock in the joined letter forms. The answer key is at the end of the unit — cover it first.
**The next day, reread yesterday's dialogue** before starting a new unit. Five minutes. This is what separates people who finish twenty units and remember them from those who finish and forget.

blocks.text: How to read the transliteration in this book

The pronunciation is written in ordinary Latin letters, not phonetic symbols. One important adjustment: **long vowels are written double.** كِتَاب becomes *kitaab*, not *kitab*. Vowel length in Arabic changes meaning — عَالَم (*'aalam*, world) and عَلَم (*'alam*, flag) are not the same word — and shortening long vowels is one of the most noticeable marks of a foreign accent. The four "heavy" (emphatic) consonants are written with a dot underneath: *ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ*. When two separate letters would otherwise look like one of the pairs *sh, th, dh, kh, gh*, a hyphen keeps them apart: *as-hal* (s + h), *idh-hab* (dh + h).

blocks.title: The one thing that helps most
items: Always read **aloud**, never silently. The difference between س and ص, or ت and ط, can't be learned with the eyes — your mouth has to feel it. Five minutes of reading aloud every day is worth more than an hour of silent reading.

front.title: The Arabic alphabet: 28 letters and their joined forms

blocks.text: If you already read fluently, a quick skim of this page is enough as a refresher — focus on the sound column, not the shapes. If you're starting from zero, stay here for two or three days before moving on to unit 1.

Arabic is written **from right to left**, and the letters join up. Each letter has up to four shapes depending on its position in the word. Six letters (ا د ذ ر ز و) can only be joined from the right — after them, the connection breaks and the next letter goes back to its initial form.
Four pairs you must tell apart
Beginners almost always merge the following pairs, and merging them changes the meaning of words. Practice one pair a day, out loud, with a hand on your throat.

head: Pair
Example
Meaning
The difference in your mouth
rows: ص: tongue spread, lips rounded, a heavy sound
ط: tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth, a thick sound
ح: from the throat, like breathing on a glass
ق: from the root of the tongue, far back

blocks.title: Taa' marbuutah — ة
items: The letter ة (at the end of a word: ـة) is not a 29th letter but a special form of ت that appears **only at the end of a word** and almost always marks **feminine gender**: مُدَرِّس (male teacher) → مُدَرِّسَة (female teacher).
How to read it: if you stop there, it's read **-ah**; if the sentence continues, it's read **-at**. In this book its pronunciation is written *-ah* when the word stands alone.
It matters far beyond politeness: ة decides the form of the adjective, the demonstrative and the verb that go with it. Misread it, and you get half the sentence wrong.

front.title: Vowel marks, tanween and reading rules

blocks.text: Arabic letters only write consonants. The vowels sit on top as small marks above and below — these are the **harakat**. Newspapers and books for adults leave them out entirely (adult readers guess them from the word pattern), but this book writes them in full from unit 1 to unit 20.
Tanween: the "a/an" marker

Tanween (a doubled vowel mark) at the end of a word marks it as **indefinite** — roughly *a book* rather than *the book*. بَيْتٌ = "a house", اَلْبَيْتُ = "the house". Note that a word with ال **never** takes tanween. Having both at once is a mistake that stands out immediately.
ال and the sun letters

اَلْ (*al-*) is the word for "the", attached to the front of a word. It's always written the same, but **not always pronounced the same**. If the next letter is one of the fourteen "sun letters" (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن), the *l* sound disappears and that letter is doubled instead.

The quickest way to remember: if the letter after ال carries a **shadda** (ّ), it's a sun letter — the *l* drops. This book always writes the shadda, so you don't need to memorize the list of fourteen.

blocks.title: Hamzat al-waṣl — the disappearing alif
items: The alif of اَلْ is not pronounced when a word comes before it. فِي + اَلْبَيْت is read *fil-bait*, not *fii al-bait*; بَيْتُ + اَلْمُدِير is read *baitul-mudiir*. That's why "Bismillaahir-rahmaanir-rahiim" flows without a break.
This book writes the pronunciation exactly as it comes out of a speaker's mouth — so don't be surprised when *al-* sometimes shows up as *-l-* in the middle of a sentence. It isn't a typo.

blocks.text: Everything the twenty units set up, gathered in one place. This page isn't meant to be read from start to finish, but to be opened when you forget.
1. Personal pronouns
2. The nominal sentence — a sentence without "is"

The pattern: **[the thing you're talking about] + [what you say about it]**. No verb at all. أَنَا طَالِبٌ = "I (am a) student". اَلْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ = "the house (is) big". Notice that the subject is almost always **definite** (with ال or a person's name), while what's said about it is **indefinite** (with tanween). If both are definite, the meaning changes: اَلْبَيْتُ اَلْكَبِيرُ = "the big house" — no longer a sentence, but a phrase.
3. Demonstratives

rows: هٰذَا كِتَابٌ — this is a book
هٰذِهِ سَيَّارَةٌ — this is a car

blocks.text: 4. Idafa — possession without "of"

Two nouns placed side by side: **[the thing] + [the owner]**. بَيْتُ اَلْمُدِيرِ = "the director's house". There's just one iron rule, and it's the one broken most often: **the first word NEVER takes ال and never takes tanween.** Only the second word takes ال. So اَلْبَيْتُ اَلْمُدِيرِ is wrong; بَيْتُ اَلْمُدِيرِ is right.
5. Adjectives agree with their noun

An adjective always comes **after** its noun and must agree with it in four ways at once: gender, definiteness, number and case. بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ (a big house) · اَلْبَيْتُ اَلْكَبِيرُ (the big house) · سَيَّارَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ (a big car) · اَلسَّيَّارَةُ اَلْكَبِيرَةُ (the big car).
6. The past tense (al-fi'l al-maaḍi)
7. The present tense (al-fi'l al-muḍaari')
Notice that **تَكْتُبُ** can mean "you (m) write" **or** "she writes". Context tells them apart — and this is one of the most common sources of misunderstanding at A1.
8. Negation

10. Numbers 1–20
11. Plurals

Arabic has two kinds of plural. The **sound plural** just adds an ending: مُسْلِم → مُسْلِمُونَ (muslimuun, masculine), مُسْلِمَة → مُسْلِمَات (muslimaat, feminine). The **broken plural** changes the inside of the word and has to be learned one by one: كِتَاب → كُتُب, بَيْت → بُيُوت, رَجُل → رِجَال, وَلَد → أَوْلَاد. Unfortunately, broken plurals are the most common.
One rule that surprises English speakers: **non-human plurals are treated as feminine singular.** اَلْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ = "the books are new" — the adjective is feminine singular, not plural.
Ordered by how often they come up in everyday conversation, not alphabetically. The forms given are: past (he) — present (he), because every other form can be derived from those two.

If you've reached this page after really working through all twenty units — not just reading them — you now have around six hundred words, the complete framework of the Arabic sentence, and the ability to read vowelled text without stumbling. That's a full A1, and that's no small thing.
What matters most now is not adding more material but **moving the language from your eyes to your mouth**. Three suggestions, ranked by results:

blocks.title: Three steps after A1
items: **Reread this whole book out loud, one unit a day, without looking at the translations.** Twenty days. It sounds boring, and it's exactly what works best: material you already understand is the only material you can say fluently.

**Move on to vowelled texts that aren't lessons.** Children's news, graded short stories, or A2 readers. Look for ones that are still vowelled — dropping the vowel marks too soon is the fastest way to lose motivation.

**Find someone to talk to before you feel ready.** You will never feel ready. Linguo's private Arabic classes start exactly here: native-speaker teachers, A2 material, and mistakes corrected before they become habits.

blocks.text: One last thing about dialects. After A1 Fusha, you'll find that Arabs on social media write in a language somewhat different from what you've learned. Don't panic and don't feel cheated: the framework you have applies to all of it. Adding Egyptian or Levantine dialect on top of solid Fusha takes weeks; doing it the other way round takes years.
مَعَ السَّلَامَة! *(ma'as-salaamah — go safely)*
